body:
Why nuclear installations require special safety measures

Nuclear energy is released when an atomic nucleus undergoes a nuclear reaction. In a nuclear power station, controlled nuclear fission produces heat, which is used to generate electricity. The process also produces radioactive substances, including fission products within the nuclear fuel.

A radioactive substance contains unstable atomic nuclei that undergo spontaneous decay and emit radiation. Some radionuclides decay quickly, while others remain radioactive for much longer periods. Nuclear safety therefore concerns both the prevention of accidents during operation and the safe management of radioactive materials after their use.

Nuclear safety means achieving proper operating conditions, preventing accidents and mitigating their consequences so that workers, the public and the environment are protected from undue radiation risks.

Nuclear safety is different from nuclear security. Safety mainly addresses accidental failures, operational hazards and unintentional exposure. Security addresses deliberate harmful acts, such as theft, sabotage and unauthorized access. Both contribute to protecting people and radioactive materials.

Radioactivity, exposure and contamination

Ionizing radiation has enough energy to remove electrons from atoms or molecules. It can damage living cells and biological molecules. The effect depends on the kind of radiation, the amount absorbed, the organs exposed and other conditions.

Important forms of nuclear radiation include alpha particles, beta particles, gamma rays and neutrons. Alpha particles have limited penetration through intact skin but can be particularly hazardous when alpha-emitting material enters the body. Gamma rays are highly penetrating electromagnetic radiation and can create an external exposure hazard.

Two terms must be distinguished:

  • Radiation exposure: Radiation reaches a person or object. The person need not become radioactive or contaminated. A medical X-ray is a familiar example of exposure without radioactive contamination.
  • Radioactive contamination: Radioactive material is present where it is not intended, such as on skin, clothing, equipment, soil or inside the body. Contaminating material may continue to cause exposure until it is removed or decays.

Radioactivity is measured in becquerels (Bq). A becquerel represents 1 nuclear disintegration per second. The sievert (Sv) is used for equivalent or effective radiation dose, quantities that account for the biological significance of radiation exposure. A large activity in Bq is not itself a measurement of the dose received by a person.

The 3 fundamental nuclear safety functions

A nuclear power station must maintain 3 basic safety functions:

  1. Control the nuclear reaction: Maintain control of reactivity and stop the fission chain reaction when required.
  2. Remove heat: Remove heat from the nuclear fuel during operation and continue removing residual heat after shutdown.
  3. Confine radioactive substances: Keep radioactive materials within designated barriers and prevent or limit their release.

The distinction between stopping the reaction and removing heat is particularly important. Even after the fission chain reaction is stopped, radioactive fission products continue to decay and release decay heat. Thus, successful shutdown does not eliminate the need for cooling.

Radiation protection in normal operation

Radiation protection follows the principle of keeping exposure as low as reasonably achievable (ALARA), taking economic and social factors into account. Workers reduce external exposure by limiting time near a source, increasing distance where feasible and using suitable shielding. Monitoring devices, controlled access and contamination checks provide further protection.

Authorized radioactive releases from facilities are controlled by regulatory limits and monitoring requirements. An authorized discharge within those limits is different from an accidental uncontrolled release. In India, AERB specifies that the additional annual dose to a member of the public from regulated discharges of an operating nuclear power plant must remain within the applicable 1 mSv limit. This is not a limit on the person's total radiation dose from all natural and medical sources.

Prelims focus

  • The 3 fundamental safety functions are control of reactivity, heat removal and confinement of radioactive material.
  • Decay heat continues after the fission chain reaction stops.
  • Becquerel measures activity; sievert is used for radiation dose.
  • ALARA concerns keeping radiation exposure as low as reasonably achievable.
  • Trap: Radiation exposure does not necessarily mean radioactive contamination.

[Sources: NCERT, Science, Class IX, Chapter 4, Structure of the Atom; NCERT, Science, Class X, Sources of Energy, subsection Nuclear Energy; Bhabha Atomic Research Centre, Safety of Nuclear Reactors, sections on safety principles and radiation protection (consulted 16 November 2026); IAEA, Licensing Process for Nuclear Installations, paragraph 3.21 (consulted 16 November 2026); Atomic Energy Regulatory Board, Radioactive Waste Management, regulatory discharge limits (consulted 16 November 2026).]

pictures.caption: Safety begins with routine inspection, monitoring and careful operation.

title: Nuclear Safety: Basic Concepts, Radiation Hazards and Safety Functions

body:
The meaning of defence in depth

No complex installation can assume that every component, instrument and human action will always perform perfectly. Nuclear safety therefore relies on defence in depth: several successive levels of protection are provided so that a single failure does not immediately lead to harmful consequences.

The levels are intended to be sufficiently independent. If an abnormal condition defeats one protection measure, another should prevent escalation or limit the consequences. Defence in depth combines sound design, reliable operation, safety systems, protective barriers and emergency preparedness.

Defence in depth is a safety approach based on successive, as far as practicable independent, levels of protection to prevent accidents and mitigate their consequences if prevention fails.

The 5 levels of defence in depth

  1. Level 1: Prevention of abnormal operation and failures. Careful site selection, suitable design, construction quality, inspection, maintenance and disciplined operating procedures aim to prevent faults from arising.
  2. Level 2: Control of abnormal operation and detection of failures. Monitoring, alarms, operating controls and protective actions detect deviations early and prevent them from developing into accidents.
  3. Level 3: Control of accidents within the design basis. Engineered safety systems respond to accidents that the plant has been specifically designed to withstand, limiting damage and maintaining essential safety functions.
  4. Level 4: Control of severe plant conditions. Additional measures seek to prevent progression to severe accidents and mitigate their consequences, including conditions that go beyond the original design-basis accident assumptions.
  5. Level 5: Mitigation of radiological consequences of significant releases. Emergency arrangements protect the public and environment if substantial radioactive material is released or threatens to be released beyond the facility.

The distinction between Levels 3 and 4 is important. Level 3 addresses accidents considered in the plant's design basis, while Level 4 deals with more severe conditions and limiting their progression. Level 5 concerns protection from radiological consequences, including measures outside the plant.

Physical barriers are not the same as the 5 levels

Defence in depth also uses physical barriers that restrict the movement of radioactive material. In a common nuclear fuel arrangement, these include:

  • Fuel material: The solid fuel matrix retains many radioactive fission products.
  • Fuel cladding: A sealed metallic covering separates the fuel from the coolant.
  • Coolant pressure boundary: The relevant vessels, tubes and piping provide another barrier against the escape of radioactive material.
  • Containment: The surrounding engineered structure provides an additional barrier against releases to the environment.

The precise construction of these barriers depends on the installation. They are not simply another name for the 5 defence-in-depth levels. A physical barrier confines material; a defence level may involve prevention, monitoring, accident control or protection of the public.

Redundancy, diversity and common-cause failure

Redundancy means providing additional equipment or capacity capable of performing the same required function. If one safety component is unavailable, another may remain available.

Diversity means using different methods or technologies to achieve a safety function, reducing dependence on a single type of equipment or failure mechanism. For example, combining powered cooling with a suitable natural-circulation cooling arrangement can provide diversity.

These protections may still be defeated by a common-cause failure: one event affects several supposedly independent systems. A flood that damages multiple backup power sources placed in the same vulnerable area illustrates this problem. Therefore, physical separation, protection from external hazards and genuinely independent arrangements matter alongside equipment numbers.

The presence of several safety levels is not permission to continue normal operation with a required level unavailable. Safety requirements govern the availability of protective measures and the conditions under which operation may continue. Any relaxation must be justified for the specific mode of operation.

Prelims focus

  • Defence in depth consists of 5 successive protection levels.
  • Level 1 prevents failures; Level 2 detects and controls abnormal operation.
  • Level 3 controls design-basis accidents; Level 4 addresses severe conditions.
  • Level 5 mitigates radiological consequences affecting people and the environment.
  • Redundancy means backup capability; diversity means different ways of providing a function.
  • Trap: Physical containment barriers and defence-in-depth levels are related but are not identical classifications.

[Sources: IAEA, Safety of Nuclear Power Plants: Design, SSR-2/1 (Rev. 1), paragraphs 2.12–2.14 and Requirement 7 (consulted 16 November 2026); IAEA, Licensing Process for Nuclear Installations, paragraphs 3.19–3.21 (consulted 16 November 2026); Bhabha Atomic Research Centre, Safety of Nuclear Reactors, defence-in-depth and physical-barrier sections (consulted 16 November 2026).]

pictures.alt: The fuel matrix sits inside sealed cladding, the coolant pressure boundary and engineered containment; these barriers differ from the 5 defence-in-depth levels.
pictures.caption: Successive physical barriers limit the escape of radioactive material.

title: Defence in Depth: Five Levels of Protection and Multiple Physical Barriers

body:
Safety systems support essential functions

Nuclear installations require arrangements that can detect unsafe conditions, stop the nuclear reaction, remove heat and prevent radioactive releases. These arrangements may rely on powered machinery, natural physical processes or a combination of both.

Safety systems are commonly distinguished as active and passive according to the way they perform their safety functions.

Active safety systems

An active safety system generally needs powered equipment, external energy, active control or mechanical operation to perform its function. Examples include electrically driven emergency cooling pumps, motor-operated valves and powered ventilation or filtration arrangements.

An active system can respond quickly and provide controlled performance. Its limitations include dependence on functioning equipment and, where required, electricity, control signals and supporting services.

Backup electricity and alternative arrangements improve the reliability of active systems. However, simply providing several powered pumps does not guarantee safety if a common event disables their shared power supply or cooling source.

Passive safety systems

A passive safety system performs its intended safety function mainly through natural physical effects rather than continuously powered machinery. Depending on the design, these effects may include gravity, natural circulation, stored pressure, condensation and heat transfer.

For example, a suitably arranged water supply may flow under gravity, while a natural-circulation system may transfer heat because of density differences between warmer and cooler fluid. Passive heat removal can be especially valuable when normal electricity supplies are lost.

Passive does not mean infallible. A passive system may still require a valve or other component to initiate operation, and its performance can depend on available water, suitable temperature differences and an adequate heat sink. Some systems combine active initiation with passive operation.

Inherent characteristics and engineered passive features

An inherent safety characteristic arises from the physical properties or behaviour of a system or material. An engineered passive safety feature is deliberately provided to use natural processes for protection. These concepts are related but not interchangeable: a system can be designed to act passively without being an inherent property of the fuel or material itself.

What happens when normal operation is interrupted?

Consider a situation in which a reactor shuts down automatically after an abnormal event. Stopping the fission chain reaction satisfies the reactivity-control function. However, the fuel still produces decay heat. The plant must therefore retain an effective heat-removal route, whether through available powered equipment, qualified passive systems or other protective arrangements.

If cooling becomes inadequate, fuel temperatures may rise even though the reactor is no longer producing its previous fission power. This explains why accident prevention requires attention to the reliability of shutdown, cooling and confinement separately.

Monitoring and protective action

Instruments provide information on relevant plant conditions, while protective systems or operating personnel may act when established limits are approached. Alarms alone do not cool the fuel or contain radioactive substances; they provide information that enables protective action. Safety consequently depends on both the reliability of equipment and the correctness of the response.

Prelims focus

  • Active systems generally depend on powered equipment or active control.
  • Passive systems mainly use natural effects such as gravity and natural circulation.
  • Loss of external electricity is an important hazard for powered cooling arrangements.
  • Decay heat removal remains necessary after reactor shutdown.
  • Trap: A passive safety feature may need an initiating action and suitable physical conditions; it is not automatically independent of every component.

[Sources: IAEA, Safety of Nuclear Power Plants: Design, SSR-2/1 (Rev. 1), discussion of passive and active safety features in defence in depth (consulted 16 November 2026); IAEA, Storage of Spent Nuclear Fuel, Annex I, paragraphs I.62–I.64 on passive heat removal (consulted 16 November 2026); Bhabha Atomic Research Centre, Safety of Nuclear Reactors, safety-system and emergency-cooling sections (consulted 16 November 2026).]

pictures.alt: Powered pumps drive active cooling; natural effects drive passive cooling, which can continue without power if conditions and the heat sink are adequate.
pictures.caption: Active and passive cooling arrangements differ mainly in what drives the cooling process.

title: Active and Passive Nuclear Safety Systems: How Protection Continues During Failures
